scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Originating in Veracruz, Mexico, the dance is linked to the Old Germanic word 'raspere'.
It gained significant popularity as a social dance after 1945 in Mexico and Cuba.
Some theories suggest it may be a descendant of European 'Strohschneider' jumping dances seen in 16th-century paintings by Pieter Bruegel.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: La Raspa is a celebratory dance used for social gatherings.
It is also a foundational piece for dance education in schools.
Historically, it has been associated with harvest or fertility themes in its ancestral forms.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance features a 'scraping' movement where dancers jump and thrust one heel forward, then quickly switch to the other.
This is typically performed in a 6/8 meter.
Partners often link elbows or hold hands to swing around during the melodic chorus sections between the scraping steps.
Watch for The Scraping Step.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (nGT4xXZ9ZkM)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Danced in pairs or a communal circle; requires enough space for elbow-link spinning.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is defined by a 6/8 time signature and the use of the Güiro, a scraper instrument that produces a ratchet-like sound.
It is often performed by folk ensembles and is a key component of the 'Mexican Hat Dance' medley.
Listen for the Güiro, Violin, Trumpet, Guitar.
The pulse is 6/8 at about 120 beats a minute.
A bright, driving 6/8 melody characterized by the prominent, rhythmic rasping sound of the Güiro scraper and brassy mariachi-style accents.

scenes.title: Step A — slowly

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
